newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Anglian pumps up profits, stems leaks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Anglian pumps up profits, stems leaks.

text.p: British water and sewerage company Anglian announced increased annual profits as expected on Wednesday and said it had cut leakage of water, less than two weeks after a "crisis summit" on the current drought was held by the new Labour government.

Anglian, the first of the much-criticised water companies to report results this year, also gained regulatory approval to buy Hartlepool Water in northeast England for 19.5 million pounds ($31.8 million), and the go-ahead to supply a commercial client outside its core area.

The company, which supplies Britain's driest area in East Anglia, said that it had cut the amount of water leaking out of its pipes to 11.8 percent from 13 percent in 1995/96 -- already one of the lowest levels in the industry.
"All the news today indicates that Anglian is one of the companies that one can believe has a good relationship with the regulator," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
"The cuts in leakage look very good as well as the approval of supplies outside its area," he added.
Anglian said pretax profits before exceptionals rose to 257 million pounds from 238.6 million and it paid out a dividend of 34.5 pence per share compared with 30 pence.
"The results were pretty much in line," the analyst said.

Anglian shares, which recently touched year-highs around 700 pence, gained ground to 695 pence before edging back to be down three pence at 679.5 pence around midsession, as the overall market lost some steam.
Anglian said it had agreed to buy Hartlepool Water for 266 pence per share with a loan note alternative and committed to cut customer bills by five percent from April 1, 2001.
The industry regulator Ofwat said that was "good news," and gave his approval to the deal.

Ofwat also announced that Anglian would be allowed to supply a chicken factory, Buxted Chicken Limited, which is outside its geographical area, in a switch from Essex & Suffolk Water, which is aimed at boosting competition.
"These are both signs that Anglian is getting on very well with the regulator, so the possibility is that it will not be hit too hard with future regulation or leakage targets," the analyst said.

The new Labour government, swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, held a summit earlier this month to tackle Britain's worst drought in 200 years and made mandatory leakage targets for companies a major plank in a 10-point plan for improvements.
Anglian's current leakage levels are seen by some observers to be close to targets which the government might set.
"This performance puts us in a good position to respond positively to the government's 10-point plan," chairman Robin Gourlay said in a statement.
The government asked companies to respond to its plan within three weeks of the summit, which was held on May 19.

Water companies are also under the spotlight as the government has vowed to impose a one-off windfall tax on the "excess profits" of privatised utilities, which have been criticised for hefty shareholder payouts and large executive pay packets.
Anglian said any tax that it paid "should be committed to the benefit of the communities we serve" in the region.
